Backdating: how mining onset years are dated, and how well

Till Meissner

2026-11-25

Summary

What this is. We want to know when mining began on land that is mined today. The embeddings classifier maps mining only from 2017 on. So we take every pixel mined in 2017 (confirmed: also mined in 2018, see diag_03_embedding_product_report), look back through the Landsat archive (1998-2018) for the year its vegetation was cleared, and impute that as the pixel’s conversion year (“onset”). Joined with the classifier’s first confirmed detections from 2018, this gives one onset series for 2000-2025, which feeds the panel.

  • Method: the Barenblitt-replica NDVI method (Section 1), with years that have only one clear image filled in from their neighbours (rule e, Section 1.3), dates every pixel mined by 2017 to an onset year, 2000-2017. The validation numbers in this summary are for the plain replica; rule e’s gain is reported in Section 2.4.
  • When imagery is good, it finds the right year: 82% of reliable pixels are dated within ±1 year of the year the embeddings classifier first detects them, with no systematic offset (mean error -0.07 yr).
  • With imagery thinned to pre-2013 sparsity: 67% within ±1 year (dated: 100%).
  • Why this method: it dates nearly every pixel, which the panel needs. LandTrendr is precise where it fires but dates only a minority of pixels, so it serves as a confidence flag (lt_agree). CCDC: see Sections 2.2 and 2.5.
  • Weak spots, flagged rather than removed: sparse early years (fake one-year dips such as the 2002 pile-up, which rule e roughly halves), pixels already bare at the start, and 2008. The persistent_loss flag separates credible dates from shaky ones (Section 2.4).
  • Two panel conventions: onsets from 2000 (main), and “no mining before 2007” (robustness; earlier onsets become a starting stock).

1. Methods

For every pixel the embeddings classifier maps as mined in 2017, we look back through the Landsat archive (1998-2018) for the year its vegetation was cleared. We use the method of Barenblitt et al. (2021), the only existing galamsey onset data, with one fix:

  1. Keep each year’s greenest NDVI value.
  2. If a year has only one clear image, replace its value with an interpolation between the neighbouring years (rule e). A single hazy image would otherwise create a fake dip.
  3. Smooth over 3 years and take the year of the largest drop as the onset.

Every pixel gets a year. The main limitation is the imagery: before 2013 a pixel has only about 1-3 clear images a year, against about 10 from 2015, so early dates are less reliable. Two flags mark this: persistent_loss (the drop lasts, it is not a one-year dip) and lt_agree (LandTrendr, a standard change-detection algorithm, finds the same year).

Two example pixels, one clean loss and one gradual (the smoothing spreads a gradual loss over several years, which is why accuracy is judged within ±1 year):

1.1 The imagery: Landsat 1998-2018

All dating methods rely on the Landsat archive, and how much imagery it holds decides how well they can work. Before 2013 a mined pixel has about 1-3 clear observations per year; from 2015 about 10. The satellites explain why. Landsat 5 was in orbit throughout, but recorded little over West Africa in the 2000s. Landsat 7 lost its scan-line corrector in May 2003, so every later scene has striped gaps. Only Landsat 8 (from 2013) brought full, regular coverage. Landsat 6 never reached orbit (1993), and Landsat 9 (2021) is after our window.

Show more: alternative methods, the method step by step, rule e and the flags

Why this method over the alternatives

Dating a land-cover change from a satellite time series is a standard problem in earth observation, and there are several ways to do it. We compare three: two widely used general-purpose change-detection algorithms, LandTrendr and CCDC, and the method Barenblitt et al. (2021) used to date galamsey in south-west Ghana. All three look for the break in a pixel’s vegetation record. They differ in how much imagery they need and in whether they always return a year.

  • LandTrendr (Kennedy et al., 2010). Reduces each year to one value (here median NBR), fits a piecewise-linear trajectory through the years, and takes the start of the largest loss segment. The loss counts only if it passes size, duration and starting-vegetation thresholds (we use Barenblitt et al.’s: magnitude > 200, duration < 4 yr, pre-value > 100). Needs: about one clear observation per year. Pro: robust to noisy single observations, and tells abrupt clearing apart from slow decline. Con: the thresholds leave most pixels undated, because gradual or partial losses on already-degraded land fail them (Section 2).
  • CCDC (Zhu & Woodcock, 2014). Uses every clear observation: it fits a seasonal model (harmonics plus trend) to each pixel and flags a break when consecutive observations stray from the model’s prediction (settings as Barenblitt et al.: minimum 3 observations, chi-square 0.8). Onset = the break with the largest NDVI drop. Needs: dense imagery, several clear observations per year, to fit the seasonal cycle and confirm a break. Pro: uses all the data and dates breaks within the year. Con: too data-hungry for the early record. With recent imagery thinned to pre-2013 density, the share of pixels it dates collapses (Section 2.2).
  • Barenblitt method (Barenblitt et al., 2021). Takes each year’s greenest NDVI value, smooths it over 3 years, and picks the year of the largest drop (details in 1.1). Needs: at least one clear observation in each of four consecutive years. Pro: dates nearly every pixel, it is simple, and it produced the only existing galamsey onset data, so ours is directly comparable. Con: there is no minimum loss, so it always picks a year, even where nothing much happened. It is sensitive to changes in how many observations a year has (the 2002 pile-up, Section 3), and the smoothing spreads a sharp loss over neighbouring years.

We deploy the Barenblitt method with one fix for single-image years (rule e, Section 1.3) and keep LandTrendr as a confidence flag (lt_agree); Section 2.5 sets out why. Naming: “Barenblitt replica” means our implementation of their method; “Barenblitt et al.” means their published data.

1.2 The Barenblitt method in detail

For every pixel mined by 2017 (in the embeddings classifier’s 2017 mask, and confirmed by its 2018 mask):

  1. Take every clear Landsat observation 1998-2018 and keep each year’s maximum NDVI.
  2. Smooth with a 3-year centred moving average.
  3. Compute the year-on-year loss in that average.
  4. The year with the largest loss is the onset year.

There is no minimum size of loss: every pixel gets a year. A year can only be scored if the pixel has clear observations in four consecutive years around it, so sparse early years limit which years can win. A clean forest-to-bare step shows up as equal losses in three consecutive years (from the smoothing). Our year label is the later one, which matches when the classifier first sees the mine (Section 2). Barenblitt et al. label the same loss one year earlier. The example figure above shows both cases: in the clean loss the largest bar is unambiguous; in the gradual loss the smoothing spreads it over several bars. Weak cases follow in Section 3.

1.3 The deployed version: rule e and the credibility flags

Step 1 takes each year’s greenest value. With several clear images a year, one hazy or cloudy image does not matter. With only one, that image is the year’s value, and if it is bad the pixel shows a fake one-year dip that step 4 then picks as the onset. Before 2013 a pixel has on average 3.5 such single-image years in 1998-2018; from 2013 almost none.

Rule e replaces the value of a single-image year by a linear interpolation between the nearest years with at least two clear images on either side. No year is dropped (dropping them removed real early onsets too and pushed every date later), and years with two or more images are untouched, so post-2013 dating is unchanged. Section 2.4 scores it.

The deployed asset also carries flags that the panel can use (full list in the appendix):

  • persistent_loss (0/1): the pixel has at least one candidate year whose loss lasts, i.e. the median annual maximum NDVI over the 3 years after it is at least 0.15 below the median over the 3 years before. A dip that recovers fails. Imagery runs to 2020 for this check only, so 2015-2017 onsets get a full 3-year window. It barely changes which year is picked, but it separates reliable dates from unreliable ones (Section 2.4).
  • onset_from2007 with loss_from2007_x1000: the same rule-e dating restricted to 2007-2017, for the “no mining before 2007” convention (2007 = start of Barenblitt et al.’s dated series). A tiny post-2007 loss means the pixel was probably mined before 2007 and belongs in the starting stock.
  • bare_pre2007: median annual maximum NDVI in 2004-2006 below 0.4, i.e. already bare going into 2007.
  • n_interp_years: how many years rule e filled in.

2. Does it find the right year?

Apart from checking pixels by hand in historical imagery (not done yet), there are two ways to judge the methods, each with a caveat:

  1. Against the classifier’s own 2018-2025 conversions (2.1, 2.2). Pixels the embeddings classifier first maps as mined in 2018-2025 have a known conversion year, independent of vegetation indices. But that year is the classifier’s first detection, not the true conversion year, and recent imagery is far denser than the early record. 2.2 therefore repeats the test with the imagery thinned to pre-2013 density.
  2. Against Barenblitt et al.’s published conversion years (classifica, 2007-2017; 2.3). These cover the real historical imagery, but they come from the same NDVI method the Barenblitt replica copies, so the comparison is tilted in its favour.

2.1 Against the classifier’s 2018-2025 conversions

Test: pixels that first appear as mined in the embeddings classifier’s masks in 2018-2025 (and were not mined in 2017) get that first-detection year as a reference. Every method is then run on 2016-2026 Landsat imagery for the same pixels. Only pixels that stay mined in every mask after first detection are scored, since their reference year is the most reliable.

2.2 The same test with sparse imagery

The same test, with each pixel’s 2016-2026 imagery randomly thinned to about 2.5 clear observations per year, the pre-2013 average (some years end up with none, as in the early record). The gaps are random, whereas real early gaps cluster in the wet season.

2.3 Against Barenblitt et al.’s conversion years

All three methods are run on the real historical imagery, on Barenblitt et al.’s own mapped footprint, so every one of their points can be scored and differences in what counts as “mined” don’t enter. Their years are shifted +1 to match our label convention (Section 1.2). Part of the Barenblitt replica’s agreement is mechanical, since it copies the method behind these years, and their years are not ground truth: they share the same imagery gaps and single-image artefacts.

2.4 Rule e and the persistent-loss flag

Rule e (Section 1.3) is judged only on the embeddings test, whose reference years do not come from NDVI. With dense imagery it changes nothing, as intended. With imagery thinned to pre-2013 density it dates a few more pixels within ±1 year and fewer 4+ years too early (a fake early dip picked as the onset). The gain is modest. It is not scored against Barenblitt et al.’s years: those share the single-image artefacts that rule e removes, so agreement with them is not the goal.

The persistent-loss flag marks which dates to trust. In the thinned test:

pixels share of pixels (%) within ±1 yr (%) ≥4 yr early (%)
no persistent loss 19.3 35.8 33.3
persistent loss 80.7 75.5 6.1

Pixels without a persistent loss are dated within ±1 year only about a third of the time. Requiring persistence does not date the remaining pixels any better than rule e; its value is in separating reliable from unreliable dates. Nationally the flag is 0 for about a third of pre-2011 onsets and 13% of 2011-2017 onsets (Section 3). The panel keeps these pixels and uses the flag for a robustness check that drops them.

2.5 Which method, then?

The panel needs an onset year for nearly every mined pixel, so what counts is the share of all pixels that are dated and dated within ±1 year, which combines coverage and accuracy:

  • Barenblitt replica (ours): 82% with dense imagery, 66% thinned to pre-2013 density (dates 100% of pixels).
  • LandTrendr: 25% with dense imagery, 18% thinned to pre-2013 density (dates 21% of pixels).
  • CCDC: 57% with dense imagery, 29% thinned to pre-2013 density (dates 39% of pixels).

The Barenblitt replica is the only method that holds up when imagery is as sparse as before 2013, because it dates almost every pixel. LandTrendr is precise where it fires but leaves most pixels undated, so it serves as a confidence flag (lt_agree). CCDC needs several clear images per year and dates few pixels once the imagery is thinned. The replica also matches the method behind the only existing galamsey onset data.

3. What the backdating shows, and its weak spots

The deployed asset covers 638,053 pixels (574 km²) mined by 2017 (confirmed in 2018), 99% of them inside Barenblitt et al.’s study area. 0.0% could not be dated. 15% are dated before 2007 (the starting stock under the robustness convention).

3.1 Our series against Barenblitt et al.’s data

Both series count new mining area per year inside Barenblitt et al.’s study area, from 2008 (their first year, shifted +1 to our label convention) to 2018. Ours is the backdated product to 2017 and the classifier’s first detections in 2018. The levels differ because the footprints differ (ours: everything the classifier maps as mined; theirs: their own map), so the shape over time is what to compare.

Correlation of new area per year, 2008-2018: r = 0.95.

3.2 The full series, 2000-2025

The backdated product (to 2017) joined with the classifier’s first confirmed detections (2018-2025). From 2017 on, both are cleaned by the temporal rule (Rule B: a status counts only when two consecutive years agree; see diag_03_embedding_product_report).

  • Bars: new mining area per year, coloured by source.
  • Line: the cumulative total of the bars, i.e. Option 1, “ever mined”: a pixel stays mined once it has been mined. This is the panel’s main spec.
  • White dots (2017-2025): Option 2, “currently mined”. The same rule, but a pixel can exit after two years in a row of “not mine”. The gap between line and dots is land mined earlier that no longer shows as mined: revegetation, flooding or abandonment, not one-year flicker, which the rule removes.
  • 2025 cannot be confirmed (no 2026 mask), so its bar is provisional.

Dashed lines mark 2007 (under the “no mining before 2007” convention, everything earlier becomes a starting stock) and the 2017/2018 seam between backdating and the classifier.

Seam check: cumulative backdated area through 2017 = 574 km², the 2017 classifier mask = 568 km² (1.2% apart; both come from the same mask, on slightly different 30 m grids).

3.3 Why early dates are weaker

The confidence flags, grouped into three onset periods:

Confidence flags by onset period, all of Ghana (area-weighted).
onset period share of dated area (%) persistent loss (%) LandTrendr agrees (%) LandTrendr disagrees (%) LandTrendr: no break (%) median loss (×1000) loss <50 (%) bare in 1998-2002 (%)
2000-2006 14.6 69.1 6.2 10.4 83.4 70 24.5 7.4
2007-2010 9.5 73.6 10.5 7.2 82.3 70 20.5 14.1
2011-2017 75.9 89.8 30.9 3.2 65.9 120 6.7 1.5

Early onsets (before 2011) are less reliable for five reasons:

  1. The loss persists less often. About two thirds of early onsets show persistent loss, against 87% from 2011 on.
  2. LandTrendr rarely confirms them. It seldom gives a different date. Mostly it finds no break that passes its own threshold, so early dates lack independent confirmation more than they face contradiction.
  3. The losses are smaller. The median early loss is about 60% of the post-2011 median, and a quarter are below 50. A small loss is where noise or ordinary farm and cocoa clearing can win the steepest-loss pick, which is the source of the “dated ≥4 years early” errors in Section 2.
  4. More pixels were already bare in 1998-2002, especially among 2007-2010 onsets. For these, the date is probably a later disturbance of an existing site, not the first mining.
  5. The design itself: no test covers onsets before 2007. The classifier ground truth starts in 2018, and Barenblitt et al.’s dates start in 2007. Also, only pixels mined in 2017 are dated, so an early site has had 10-17 years to regrow and be disturbed again, which gives several candidate losses where a late site usually has one.

3.4 Weak spots, by example

Most weak spots trace back to the sparse early imagery (Section 1.1). Three example pixels: a one-year dip (a single low observation creates a false onset, the cause of the 2002 pile-up), a pixel that was already bare at the start (no real loss to find), and a pixel dated years before Barenblitt et al.’s year.

Weak spot What we see How it’s handled
Already bare in 1998-2002 3.9% of dated area nationally; smaller losses; real onset may predate the series flag start_ndvi_x1000; bare_pre2007 sends such pixels to the starting stock under the “from 2007” convention
Few computable years some pixels choose from only a handful of candidate years flag n_computable_years, n_obs_years
2002 pile-up 7.4% of onsets with the plain replica (0.5% in 2001). A single-image artefact: 57% of 2002 pixels have only one clear image in 2003, the first Landsat 7 SLC-off year, against 17% of other pixels, and the median NDVI dips 0.81 → 0.44 → 0.76 (notes/archive/diag_06_onset_2002_check.R). The same one-year dips make up 40-60% of all onsets before 2012 rule e (deployed): 2002 falls to about 4.2% of onsets, with half of the 2002 pixels moving, mostly to 2005 or later (diag_06 sample); the rest keep a 2002 date and are flagged where the loss does not persist (persistent_loss). Nationally 2002 is still 4.6% of dated area, about 1.7× its neighbours. A likely cause: rule e only fixes years with exactly one image, so a 2003 with two or three images that are all low (dry-season-only dates, haze, partly masked cloud) still gives a dip. Before 2007, so it is in the starting stock under both conventions
2008 (and 2009) Still present with rule e: 2008 has 9.7 km², about half its neighbours, and 28% of it was already bare in 1998-2002 (2009: 18%; 2004-2007: 4-7%). With no real loss to find, the steepest-loss pick lands on a small fluctuation, and these land in 2008/09 more often than in other years. Cause not established: possibly noisy annual values in the Landsat 7 SLC-off years, when Landsat 5 recorded little over West Africa. An earlier check found Barenblitt et al.’s data often date these pixels much later (not yet re-run on the rule-e asset) persistent_loss does not catch it (68%, normal). The bare-at-start flag does: under the “from 2007” convention, bare_pre2007 sends such pixels to the starting stock
Smaller losses before 2011 sparser imagery or more gradual early clearing no minimum-loss threshold: it would cut early years far more and make mining look later

4. Settings and why

Setting Value Why
Anchor footprint embeddings mask, mined in 2017 and 2018 (Rule B) one-off 2017 blips get no onset year; 2018+ onsets come from the classifier directly
Onset window 2000-2017 2017 was cut off before (8.9% “undatable”)
Imagery 1998-2018, full year (to 2020 for the persistence check only) the 3-yr average needs a year either side; shortening it would misdate early mining
Single-image years interpolated from the nearest ≥2-image years (rule e) removes fake one-year dips without dropping any year (Sections 1.3, 2.4)
Year label later year of the loss matches the classifier’s first detection (Section 2)
Minimum loss none no natural cut-off; a threshold biases the timeline
Persistent loss 3-yr median after ≥ 0.15 below 3-yr median before flag only; separates credible from shaky dates
Later convention onsets from 2007 start of Barenblitt et al.’s dated series
LandTrendr (cross-check) mag > 200, dur < 4, pre-value > 100 Barenblitt et al.’s comparison settings
